scope: Verified framework evidence for a 45–50 minute introductory and motivation tutorial. Detailed utility use cases belong in a separate practical tutorial.
headline_recommendation: Use ToolUniverse as the main Harvard-developed framework example, followed by POPPER and/or TxAgent as research patterns. Present LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK and Google ADK as current documented development frameworks. Do not imply university affiliation proves utility readiness.

harvard_candidates.name: ToolUniverse
harvard_candidates.attribution: Harvard Medical School / Zitnik Lab-led research platform, with Harvard College, Kempner Institute, Harvard Data Science Initiative, Broad Institute, MIT and MIT Lincoln Laboratory affiliations in the paper.
harvard_candidates.authors: Shanghua Gao, Richard Zhu, Pengwei Sui, Zhenglun Kong, Sufian Aldogom, Yepeng Huang, Ayush Noori, Reza Shamji, Krishna Parvataneni, Theodoros Tsiligkaridis, Marinka Zitnik.
harvard_candidates.affiliation_evidence: Paper v3 first page: Gao is affiliation 1 (Department of Biomedical Informatics, Harvard Medical School); corresponding author Zitnik is affiliations 1, 5, 6, 7 (HMS, Kempner, Broad, HDSI).
harvard_candidates.publication: ToolUniverse: An open platform for democratizing AI scientists; arXiv:2509.23426; first submitted 2025-09-27, v3 revised 2026-08-07.
harvard_candidates.maturity: Open-source scientific-tool platform with public documentation, Python/API/MCP interfaces and tagged releases; manuscript describes v1.3.1. Cited paper is a preprint. Sources do not establish utility deployment or a safety-certified operational runtime.
harvard_candidates.verified_summary: Provides typed tool specifications and modules to register, find, call, compose, create and refine scientific tools. This makes tool integration a reusable layer around a model.
harvard_candidates.preferred_slide_wording: Harvard Medical School's ToolUniverse organizes scientific tools behind common interfaces so agents can discover, call and combine them.
harvard_candidates.count_policy: Omit tool counts on main slides. If needed: the 2025-10-09 Kempner article reports 600+; paper v3 reports 2,700+ tools as of July 2026. Current documentation contains both 1000+ and 2700+ text, so date and source any number explicitly.
harvard_candidates.utility_connection_as_inference: The transferable pattern is an approved catalog of historian, document and simulation tools with validated inputs and structured outputs; these sources do not provide utility-specific tools.

harvard_candidates.name: TxAgent
harvard_candidates.attribution: Harvard Medical School / Zitnik Lab research agent with MIT Lincoln Laboratory collaboration; author affiliations also include Brigham and Women's Hospital, Kempner, Broad and HDSI.
harvard_candidates.authors: Shanghua Gao, Richard Zhu, Zhenglun Kong, Ayush Noori, Xiaorui Su, Curtis Ginder, Theodoros Tsiligkaridis, Marinka Zitnik.
harvard_candidates.affiliation_evidence: Paper first page and official project page explicitly map most authors to Department of Biomedical Informatics, Harvard Medical School; Tsiligkaridis to MIT Lincoln Laboratory.
harvard_candidates.publication: TxAgent: An AI Agent for Therapeutic Reasoning Across a Universe of Tools; arXiv:2503.10970; submitted 2025-03-14.
harvard_candidates.maturity: Biomedical research agent/model with public code, model assets, demos and author-reported benchmark results. The cited 2025 version is a preprint, not a general production orchestration runtime. Do not infer clinical outcomes or utility performance.
harvard_candidates.verified_summary: Combines a domain-specialized model, ToolRAG retrieval and ToolUniverse to select tools, retrieve biomedical evidence and iteratively answer therapeutic reasoning tasks.
harvard_candidates.preferred_slide_wording: TxAgent shows a domain agent selecting relevant tools, retrieving evidence and revising its answer across multiple steps.
harvard_candidates.count_policy: The original 2025 paper's 211-tool toolbox describes that experiment, not today's ToolUniverse library size. Avoid mixing the two counts.
harvard_candidates.utility_connection_as_inference: The lesson is that an operations agent needs curated domain tools and evidence checks; a large general model alone does not provide the full workflow.

harvard_candidates.name: POPPER
harvard_candidates.attribution: Stanford–Harvard research collaboration. Harvard affiliation is specifically co-first author Ying Jin at the Data Science Initiative and Department of Health Care Policy; other author department affiliations in the paper are Stanford.
harvard_candidates.authors: Kexin Huang, Ying Jin, Ryan Li, Michael Y. Li, Emmanuel Candès, Jure Leskovec.
harvard_candidates.affiliation_evidence: First page lists Ying Jin as affiliation 2: Data Science Initiative & Department of Health Care Policy, Harvard University.
harvard_candidates.publication: Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications; ICML 2025, PMLR 267:25372–25437; conference July 13–19, 2025. arXiv first submitted 2025-02-14.
harvard_candidates.maturity: Peer-reviewed research framework with public implementation, benchmark scripts and demo. It is a hypothesis-testing research system, not a utility operations runtime.
harvard_candidates.verified_summary: An experiment-design agent proposes falsification tests, an execution agent runs analyses, and sequential evidence aggregation controls false-positive claims under the paper's stated assumptions.
harvard_candidates.preferred_slide_wording: POPPER, a Stanford–Harvard collaboration, separates proposing a hypothesis from executing tests and deciding whether the evidence supports it.
harvard_candidates.limitations: Formal Type-I error control relies on valid logical implications, sequential statistical validity and stopping assumptions. It is not a blanket guarantee for LLM outputs or physical safety.
harvard_candidates.utility_connection_as_inference: Teach 'an explanation is a hypothesis; an independent tool test supplies evidence.' Do not claim POPPER has validated feeder control or transmission dispatch.

development_frameworks.name: LangGraph
development_frameworks.role: Stateful workflow graphs combining deterministic code and agentic steps, with persistence and human oversight.
development_frameworks.teaching_visual: A small graph with retrieve → analyze → verify → review and a bounded retry edge.
development_frameworks.utility_connection: Implement an explicit advisory workflow; engineering tools supply numerical validation.
development_frameworks.connection_status: Educational design inference, not a named deployment.

development_frameworks.name: Microsoft Agent Framework
development_frameworks.role: Agents and graph-based workflows, tool integration, middleware and resumable checkpoints.
development_frameworks.teaching_visual: Agent cards inside a workflow, with a checkpoint/database icon.
development_frameworks.utility_connection: Long-running case triage and handover require durable, protected state.
development_frameworks.connection_status: Educational design inference, not a named deployment.

development_frameworks.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
development_frameworks.role: Code-first tools, specialist handoffs, guardrails, review and tracing in the application's runtime.
development_frameworks.teaching_visual: One coordinator calling three typed tools, with a visible action trace.
development_frameworks.utility_connection: Expose narrow approved read/simulate/draft functions and evaluate observable actions.
development_frameworks.connection_status: Educational design inference, not a named deployment.

development_frameworks.name: Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)
development_frameworks.role: Agent and graph workflows, human input, structured routing and evaluation; ADK 2.0 is documented for 2026.
development_frameworks.teaching_visual: A graph with deterministic input checks before an agent and evaluator after it.
development_frameworks.utility_connection: Validate asset identity and tool trajectory in replayed scenarios.
development_frameworks.connection_status: Educational design inference, not a named deployment.

recommended_slides.title: Frameworks give the agent a working environment
recommended_slides.visual: Four compact cards: LangGraph (state/graph), Microsoft (workflow/checkpoint), OpenAI (tools/handoffs/traces), Google ADK (agents/graphs/evaluation).
recommended_slides.caption: Current documented framework examples; compare fit through local evaluation.
recommended_slides.key_message: A model proposes the next step; the surrounding application supplies tools, state, policy and observable results.

recommended_slides.title: Harvard example: ToolUniverse
recommended_slides.visual: Original static schematic: goal → tool finder → typed tool caller → scientific resources; structured results return to the agent. Add manager/composer as small supporting blocks.
bullets: Developed by a Harvard Medical School-led team with collaborators.
Standardizes how an agent discovers, calls and combines scientific tools.
The reusable idea: governed interfaces and testable outputs.
Research platform; utility deployment needs its own tools and validation.

recommended_slides.title: Research lesson: specialize the tools, test the claim
recommended_slides.visual: Two lanes: TxAgent — request → relevant tools → evidence-based response; POPPER — hypothesis → designed test → executed analysis → evidence decision.
bullets: TxAgent: a Harvard-led biomedical agent with domain tools.
POPPER: a Stanford–Harvard framework for hypothesis testing.
Transfer the design lessons: curate evidence and test proposed explanations.
Benchmarks support research claims within their evaluated tasks.

lecture_guidance: Keep this framework segment to about 8–9 minutes in the 45–50 minute introductory session.
Use static original diagrams and at most one progressive reveal per diagram; avoid motion between every slide.
A single utility teaser can motivate the tool pattern; reserve detailed operator prompts, simulation settings and three full cases for the separate practical tutorial.
Provide full paper titles, dates, official documentation and code URLs in a reading list; a logo and short author-year label are not a full reading source.
The Harvard Kempner computing handbook lists common frameworks, but inclusion there is not evidence Harvard developed those frameworks.
Avoid broad claims that more tools, more agents or a more prestigious institution makes a deployment safer or more effective.
